name: Nightshade
blurb: A twin-engine stealth fighter built around one idea: see first, shoot first, never be seen. Every edge is aligned to a few shared angles so radar returns are concentrated into narrow spikes instead of a glow.
aero: Planform alignment: wing leading edges, stabilators and fin edges share 42° sweep, so radar energy reflects into a few narrow directions.
Chined forward fuselage blends into the wing and generates body lift and vortex flow at high angle of attack.
Caret intakes with serpentine ducts hide the engine faces; 2-D vectoring nozzles add pitch control below stall speed (60° alpha, demonstrated).
High dry thrust and an area-ruled, clean airframe (all weapons internal) give supercruise without afterburner.
Relaxed static stability (−8% MAC subsonic) with quadruplex fly-by-wire.
engines: 2 × afterburning low-bypass turbofan with 2-D thrust vectoring, 156 kN class
cockpit_desc: One 20×8 in panoramic touch display split into portals, a wide-angle HUD and a small digital standby display. Imperial units (knots, feet).

name: Bobcat
blurb: Small, cheap, single-engine and brutally agile. A relaxed-stability fly-by-wire jet that turns harder than it has any right to and fits a wingtip missile on each side.
aero: Blended wing-body: the wing root fairs into the fuselage, adding internal fuel volume and body lift while cutting wetted area.
Long, sharp strakes (LERX) shed vortices that keep the wing flying up to 25° alpha.
Fixed chin intake sits under the fuselage, so the forebody straightens the airflow into it at high alpha; a fixed inlet keeps weight down but limits it to about Mach 2.
Relaxed static stability (about −4% MAC) with fly-by-wire and a side-stick; g-limit 9 with an alpha limiter at 25°.
Bubble canopy with no frame ahead of the pilot for an all-round view.
radar: Mechanically scanned pulse-Doppler (AESA in late blocks)
cockpit_desc: HUD with an up-front control panel, two 4×4 in monochrome MFDs, analog standby attitude/airspeed/altitude, RWR scope and side-stick. Imperial units.

name: Sirocco
blurb: A pan-European canard delta: unstable on purpose, light for its size and built to climb and accelerate. Its foreplanes are placed so their wake never disturbs the main wing at high alpha.
aero: Close-coupled canard delta: the all-moving foreplanes ahead of the wing make the jet strongly unstable subsonic (about −15% MAC), which quadruplex fly-by-wire turns into fast pitch response and low trim drag.
With the canard providing nose-up pitch, the delta wing trims with trailing edges down: lift is added, not subtracted as with a tailplane.
Ventral "smile" intake with variable lower lip stays fed at high alpha because the forward fuselage shields it.
53° delta: low wave drag and large internal fuel volume; supercruise around Mach 1.3 clean.
Wingtip pods carry defensive-aid sensors and help as end-plates.
cockpit_desc: Three full-colour head-down displays (MHDD), wide HUD, glareshield warning panel, digital standby. Imperial units, NATO style.

name: Gladan
role: All-weather fighter for dispersed road bases
blurb: Designed to fly from 500 m of country road and land on the same, run by conscripts with a toolbox. A big flapped foreplane and a thrust reverser make it the short-field specialist of the group.
aero: Fixed canard with trailing-edge flaps sits above and ahead of the main wing; its vortex energises the wing upper surface, giving high lift for short take-off and landing.
Double-delta main wing with a dog-tooth: the notch creates a vortex that stops spanwise flow and keeps the outer wing from stalling first.
Thrust reverser in the engine tail cone, with automatic deployment at nose-wheel touchdown, cuts the landing roll to about 500 m.
Efficient afterburning turbofan (derived from an airliner core) gives long range for a 1970s single-engine fighter.
Conventional (stable) design with an analog autopilot; 7.5 g limit set by the long-range fuel load.
engines: 1 × afterburning turbofan with thrust reverser, 125 kN class
cockpit_desc: 1970s analog: early HUD, round radar display (CI) in the centre, metric instruments (km/h, metres) with Swedish-style labels.

name: Tianlong
blurb: A long, heavy stealth canard-delta built to reach far out over the sea and hit tankers and radar planes with very long-range missiles. Range and endurance were chosen over dogfighting.
aero: Long chined fuselage holds a large internal fuel load (11 t) and a deep main weapon bay.
All-moving canards with dihedral plus LERX create a vortex system over the delta wing, so the large, low-loaded wing keeps lift at high alpha.
Bump-type (diverterless) intakes shed the boundary layer without a moving part or a radar-reflecting gap.
All-moving canted fins plus small ventral fins keep directional stability at Mach 2 despite the long nose.
Relaxed stability with triplex digital fly-by-wire.
cockpit_desc: One very wide colour LCD flanked by small touch displays, wide-angle HUD. Metric units, Chinese and English labels.

name: Strizh
blurb: A short-range, twin-engine dogfighter built to operate from rough frontline strips. Wide-set engines under a lifting body, huge LERX and a helmet-cued IR missile make it lethal inside visual range.
aero: Integral layout: widely spaced engine nacelles under a flat lifting body. About 40% of the lift comes from the fuselage.
Large, sharply swept LERX create vortex lift up to about 30° alpha and keep the twin fins in clean air.
Wedge intakes under the LERX are fed in clean flow at high alpha; on the ground, doors close them and dorsal louvres breathe for the engines to avoid ingesting debris.
Twin canted fins and stabilators give strong control power; conventional stability with a mechanical/analog control system.
Fuel is limited (3.5 t internal), which is the price of its agility and short-field ability.
cockpit_desc: Analog Soviet-style: turquoise panel, metric instruments, ADI with moving aircraft symbol, combined AoA/g gauge, dual-needle airspeed and altitude, Cyrillic labels.

name: Grifon
blurb: Big, fast and able to point its nose anywhere: three-axis thrust vectoring and movable leading-edge root extensions let it fly well past the stall and recover. Stealth shaping is partial; agility and range are the priority.
aero: Widely spaced engines with a flat lifting body between them; weapon bays sit in tandem in the tunnel between the nacelles.
LEVCONs (movable leading-edge root extensions) act like canards to control the vortex at high alpha without a canard's radar return.
Three-axis thrust vectoring allows post-stall manoeuvres (above 70° alpha) and helps trim at supersonic speed.
All-moving fins that are small for the size of the jet reduce side-on radar return.
Large internal fuel (10.3 t) gives long range without tanks; the airframe is unstable and the fly-by-wire is fully digital.
engines: 2 × afterburning turbofan with 3-D thrust vectoring, 147 kN class
radar: AESA nose + side-looking AESAs, L-band LEVCON arrays
cockpit_desc: Two large 15 in colour displays, side displays, wide HUD, metric units and Cyrillic labels.

name: Cormorant
blurb: My own pick: a two-seat, variable-sweep naval interceptor. Wings forward it lands slowly on a carrier; wings back it dashes past Mach 2 to shoot long-range missiles at bombers 150 km out.
aero: Variable sweep (20°–68°), scheduled by a computer to Mach: high aspect ratio and big flaps for carrier approach, low drag fully swept for the dash.
Wide, flat "pancake" body between the nacelles produces lift and carries four long-range missiles semi-recessed underneath.
Glove vanes and highly swept fixed gloves move the centre of lift forward at high Mach and offset the aft shift of the aerodynamic centre that comes with sweeping the wings.
Widely spaced engines: one engine failing does not take out the other; ramped 2-D intakes allow Mach 2.3+.
Twin canted fins and big stabilators (used differentially for roll at high sweep).
cockpit_desc: 1970s US Navy analog: VDI and HSD CRTs, tape-and-dial instruments, wing-sweep indicator, AoA indexer for carrier landing, early stroke HUD. Imperial units.
